overview: Oirat leaders built changing alliances within the Mongolian world, sometimes challenging its khans and sometimes cooperating with them. This atlas shows only 1492 to 1530. Its outline is displaced far north into Siberia and misses much of the Altai and Dzungarian setting; it should not be read as a reliable boundary. Earlier power under Esen and later Oirat cultural achievements are dated separately below.

periods.title: The atlas phase
periods.summary: Oirat communities faced renewed eastern Mongol power during the age of Dayan Khan.

sections.title: Power, diplomacy and the map’s short window

items.text: The membership of the “Four Oirats” changed. Powerful chiefs lacked descent from Chinggis Khan, which mattered in disputes over their right to become khans.

Before this map phase, Esen’s forces defeated the Ming army at Tumu in 1449 and captured the emperor Zhu Qizhen. Capturing an emperor was an extraordinary political opportunity, but it did not turn the Oirats into rulers of all China. The episode reveals how dangerous a mobile northern coalition could be to an enormous settled empire.

In 1453 Esen announced his own claim to the Yuan throne. A letter recorded by Ming officials invoked the old dynasty, its people and its imperial jade seal. Historian Hidehiro Okada uses this document to show that the loss of China in 1368 had not ended claims to Yuan legitimacy. A seal could be a powerful political argument.

The 1492 to 1530 map window belongs to a different balance of power. By about 1510, Dayan Khan had reunited the eastern Mongols and removed the taishi office that strongmen had used to dominate khans. Oirat communities survived these reversals; later sixteenth-century campaigns against them continued.

Diplomacy involved competing descriptions of authority. In 1488 Dayan Khan sent a Mongolian letter demanding reception for his envoys and calling himself Grand Khan of the Great Yuan. Ming records preserve that claim. Reading such letters alongside later chronicles helps historians separate contemporary assertions from stories written generations afterward.

sections.title: Horses, markets and a glimpse inside a camp

items.text: Fifteenth-century Oirat missions brought horses, camels and furs to Ming China and received valuable textiles. At Beijing’s Huitongguan guesthouse, envoys could exchange luxury rewards for everyday necessities. Diplomacy therefore carried shopping lists as well as grand titles. Muslim merchants also travelled with these missions, connecting Oirat power to Hami and wider Central Asian trade.

An official horse market opened near Datong in 1438. Trade also included items Ming authorities tried to restrict, such as ironware and weapons. A horse breeder, a merchant and a government official could want very different things from the same market. Commercial restrictions were part of the rivalry that preceded Esen’s invasion.

The Ming interpreter Ha Ming, later called Yang Ming, describes life around the captive emperor in 1449. He and his father obtained a skin bag of mare’s milk, searched for rice and flour, and exchanged clothing for a sheep. These are unusually concrete glimpses of camp provisions, although an imperial prisoner’s meals were not an ordinary family’s daily ration.

His Chinese account calls the milk container “馬乳一皮袋”, translated here as “one skin bag of mare’s milk”. In modern Mandarin reading, that is mǎ rǔ yī pí dài. The phrase records an object in an Oirat camp through a Ming servant’s Chinese narrative; it is not an Oirat-language sentence. A flexible bag made more sense on a journey than a kitchen cupboard.

sections.title: Later Oirat households and practical rules, in 1640

items.text: The Mongol-Oirat Great Code of 1640 belongs more than a century after this map ends. Its household provisions discuss respect for elders and assistance between relatives at weddings. Family relationships carried economic duties, as well as affection and ceremony. These are rules lawmakers wanted people to follow, not proof that every household behaved identically.

The later code rewarded someone who extinguished a fire left at an abandoned camp with a sheep. It also provided rewards for rescuing people, livestock and felt tents from danger. Moving camp did not make a neglected fire someone else’s harmless problem.

Another 1640 rule addressed help during childbirth or illness: a successful helper should receive the promised reward, or a horse if none had been agreed. The same section rewards rescuing animals stuck in mud. It records the value placed on practical assistance, but supplies neither a medical recipe nor evidence for camp toilets.

sections.title: Later books, discoveries and a small Oirat word

items.text: Zaya Pandita developed Clear Script in 1648, long after this atlas phase. It supported Buddhist translation into Oirat and became an important literary medium. It must not be placed in a scene dated 1500. Cambridge’s cultural-heritage project documents readers and collectors who still discuss and preserve this tradition.

At the later monastery of Ablaikit, excavations in 2016 to 2019 recovered small birch-bark manuscript fragments. Three belong to a Heart Sutra book measuring about 5 by 10 centimetres, written in black ink. It was almost pocket-sized. Its proposed early date, 1648 to 1657, depends on deliberate burial during construction; disturbed deposits allow a later date, possibly into the 1710s.

A tiny writing sample from that Oirat Heart Sutra is “tegēd”, meaning “after that”. This is the scholar’s Latin-letter transcription of Clear Script on folio 13 recto, line 10, rather than a recreation of its damaged letters. The same word and translation are identified in another seventeenth-century manuscript, Mong. K 38. The sample belongs to later Oirat literary history, not 1492.

Ablaikit’s surviving books also reveal people learning from other people’s handwriting. In one manuscript, the pen changes between an Oirat style and a more formal Mongolian style. Yampolskaya suggests that one scribe was demonstrating a technique and another trying to copy it. This is an interpretation of the strokes, a rare possible glimpse of a lesson rather than a school attendance register.

The later fortified monastery was founded by the Khoshut leader Ablai in the 1650s. Research on its archives places his dealings with Muscovy within hopes of profiting from trade with China. Oirat politics still involved several competing leaders; calling every local ruler “Dzungar” can conceal Khoshut power. Later visitors found books among the ruins, while settlers reused building materials.

Oirat political history continued through different seventeenth-century centres, including Dzungaria, the Khoshut realm around Qinghai, and the Kalmyk polity near the Volga. Their laws changed with migration, rulers and relations with neighbouring empires. Those branches should be studied in their own periods, rather than stretched backward into one unchanging confederation.

ending.text: The map’s cutoff in 1530 is not a documented collective disappearance. Oirat coalitions endured military setbacks, regrouped and developed new political centres. Communities of Oirat ancestry and cultural affiliation continue in Mongolia, China and Russia.
